questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Openings that name a disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Identify when an opening names the disagreement
questions.stem: In a city planner's memo, a paragraph opens by stating the dispute before giving background. What does this opening achieve?

options.text: It names the disagreement so the reader knows what is at stake.

options.misconception: assumes background must precede any statement of conflict

options.text: It proves the author's position is correct before presenting evidence.

options.text: It removes the need for evidence by framing the issue emotionally.
options.misconception: treats framing as a substitute for supporting reasons

questions.explanation: Naming the disagreement early tells the reader what is at stake. Delaying it or treating framing as proof would misread the move.
questions.hint: Ask what the opening makes visible first.

questions.topic: Reading a closing for commitment
questions.learningObjective: Read a closing for genuine commitment
questions.stem: A closing says 'we hope to revisit this soon.' Does it commit to action?

options.text: Yes, because it mentions revisiting.
options.misconception: confuses a hope with a commitment

options.text: No, because revisiting is always pointless.
Yes, because it sets a deadline.
options.misconception: reads an unspecified soon as a deadline

options.text: No, because hope is not a plan or owner.

questions.explanation: Hope without a plan, owner, or date is not a commitment. It leaves action unassigned.
questions.hint: Look for owner, action, and date.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that only relocates the disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Spot a synthesis that merely relocates disagreement
questions.stem: A synthesis moves the dispute from the plan to the budget but resolves nothing. What is the flaw?

options.text: It relocates the disagreement without resolving it.
It is too focused on the budget.
It proves the plan was correct all along.
It removes the disagreement from the record.

questions.explanation: Moving the dispute changes its location, not its substance. A real synthesis must resolve something.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything was actually resolved.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Openings that name a disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Identify an opening that names a disagreement
questions.stem: A memo from planner Elena opens with 'We disagree about whether the plaza needs shade.' What does this opening do?

options.text: It delays the main point unnecessarily.
options.misconception: misreads a direct opening as delay

options.text: It proves Elena's view is correct.
It states the dispute so readers know the issue.
It removes the need for evidence.

questions.explanation: The opening names the disagreement directly. It neither proves a view nor removes the need for evidence.
questions.hint: Notice what the first sentence makes clear.

questions.topic: Counterarguments aimed at a nearby claim

questions.stem: Why does a counterargument aimed at a nearby claim fail to move the discussion?

answer.exemplar: It leaves the actual claim untouched, so the author can dismiss it as irrelevant while the real position stands.

questions.explanation: A misplaced counterargument misses its target. The real claim survives untouched.
questions.hint: Check whether the target is the actual claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rebuttable and non-rebuttable claims
questions.learningObjective: Classify claims as rebuttable or not

stimulus.body: The memo states that the new library will open in March and that libraries are essential to democracy.

questions.stem: Which statement is rebuttable with evidence?

options.text: That libraries are essential to democracy.
options.misconception: treats a value claim as testable

options.text: Neither statement, since plans change.
Both statements, since both appear in a memo.
options.misconception: assumes memo claims are all testable

options.text: That the new library will open in March.

questions.explanation: The opening date is testable. The value claim about democracy is not directly rebuttable.
questions.hint: Ask which can be checked against facts.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Tone that closes a discussion
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a closing tone
questions.stem: A memo from planner Omar ends 'No further comment is needed.' What effect does this have?

options.text: It invites careful review of the evidence.
It proves the argument is airtight.
It signals the matter is settled and ends reply.
It shortens the memo without changing meaning.

questions.explanation: The phrase ends reply. It does not invite review or prove the argument.
questions.hint: Notice whether a response is welcome.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Questions used as assertions
questions.learningObjective: Identify a rhetorical question
questions.stem: A memo asks 'Can anyone deny the park will help children?' What is this question doing?

options.text: It invites a genuine debate about children's benefits.
It defers the decision to a later meeting.
It requests a survey of children's needs.
options.misconception: treats the question as a literal data request

options.text: It asserts the benefit without offering evidence.

questions.explanation: The question presumes its answer. It advances a claim without support.
questions.hint: Ask whether an answer is truly sought.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Disagreements about facts and about values
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish factual and value disagreement
questions.stem: Planners disagree over whether a trail will be used daily and over whether daily use justifies the cost. Which is which?

options.text: Usage is factual; justification is a value judgment.
Both are value questions.
options.misconception: treats a factual prediction as a value

options.text: Both are factual questions.
options.misconception: treats a value judgment as factual

options.text: Usage is a value; justification is factual.

questions.explanation: Daily use is measurable; whether it justifies cost is a value judgment.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence could settle each.

answer.exemplar: It helps when it corrects a misunderstanding before it spreads; it harms when it derails a point already understood.

questions.explanation: Helpful interruption removes confusion early. Harmful interruption derails understood points.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Shared premises inside a disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Find shared premises

stimulus.body: Two planners dispute whether to build a garage or a transit hub, yet both agree the downtown needs more capacity.

questions.stem: What premise do the planners share?

options.text: That neither option will work.
That garages are always cheaper.
options.misconception: states a disputed claim as shared

options.text: That transit hubs are always better.
options.misconception: states a disputed claim as shared

options.text: That downtown needs more capacity.

questions.explanation: Both plans assume downtown needs more capacity. The dispute is about means, not that premise.
questions.hint: Find the goal both accept.

questions.topic: Quoting the person you disagree with
questions.learningObjective: Quote fairly before replying
questions.stem: Why should a reply quote the opponent before responding?

options.text: It removes the need to paraphrase.
It proves the opponent contradicts themselves.
It fixes the target and prevents misrepresentation.
It makes the reply more persuasive by length.

questions.explanation: Quoting first fixes the target. It keeps the reply honest and prevents straw versions.
questions.hint: Ask what the quote fixes.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A standard of proof changed mid-argument
questions.learningObjective: Detect a shifted proof standard
questions.stem: A memo demands peer review for a rival's data but cites a blog for its own. What flaw is this?

options.text: It shows the author has no standards.
It uses too many sources for the rival.
It proves blogs are always unreliable.
It applies a stricter bar to the rival than to itself.

questions.explanation: The standard shifts between the two sides. Fair argument holds both to the same bar.
questions.hint: Compare the evidence bar on each side.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Concessions that cost more than they gain
questions.learningObjective: Identify costly concessions
questions.stem: A planner concedes the rival's budget estimate is exact and then disputes the plan's value. What risk does this create?

options.text: It makes the reply shorter.
It proves the budget estimate is wrong.
options.misconception: reads concession as evidence of error

options.text: It surrenders the strongest objection and weakens the reply.
It ends the dispute immediately.
options.misconception: treats one concession as ending debate

questions.explanation: Conceding the strongest point hands the opponent leverage. A smaller concession costs less.
questions.hint: Ask what the concession gives away.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What evidence would have been worth having
questions.learningObjective: Identify missing valuable evidence
questions.stem: A memo claims a new transit line will cut delays but cites no ridership data. What evidence would have helped?

answer.exemplar: Ridership and on-time performance data from a comparable line would have tested the claim instead of leaving it as assertion.

questions.explanation: Direct measurement of the claimed effect beats assertion. Without it the claim rests on assumption.

questions.topic: Naming what a reply actually attacks
questions.learningObjective: Name the true target of a reply

options.text: The study's method and sample.
options.misconception: confuses attacking employer with attacking method

options.text: The data tables in the report.
The conclusion about parking demand.

questions.explanation: The reply attacks the author's credibility, not method or data. Naming this keeps the argument honest.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Synthesis that changes both positions
questions.learningObjective: Recognize synthesis revising both sides
questions.stem: A synthesis keeps both original plans unchanged and only lists them side by side. Why is this not a true synthesis?

options.text: It is too short to count.
It includes too many sources.
It changes neither position, so no new view emerges.
It proves both are equally valid.
options.misconception: reads a list as equivalence proof

questions.explanation: A true synthesis revises both positions into a new view. Merely listing them leaves the disagreement intact.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything changed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Duties after being persuaded
questions.learningObjective: State a duty after persuasion
questions.stem: A planner is persuaded by new evidence and switches to supporting the rival plan. What duty follows?

options.text: No duty, since persuasion ends the matter.
The planner must reject future evidence against the new view.
The planner must hide the change to save face.
The planner must announce the change and explain why.

questions.explanation: Being persuaded creates a duty to say so and why. Hiding the change or closing inquiry betrays the discussion.

questions.topic: Norms and the mechanisms that enforce them

questions.topic: Standards of proof across settings

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish committing close from summary

A restatement of the opposing view.
A list of sources for reading.

questions.topic: Sequence for entering someone else's argument
questions.learningObjective: Order steps for entering another's argument
questions.stem: Before replying to a colleague's plan, a planner should first do what?

State their own alternative immediately.
Attack the weakest part of the plan.
Ask for more data regardless of need.

questions.explanation: Restating first ensures the reply targets the actual position. Proposing or attacking first risks a straw man.
questions.hint: Begin by showing you understood.
